name: hash-wasm
baseline: Pure-JavaScript hash libraries in V8 (crypto-js, spark-md5, jsSHA, noble-hashes, node-forge, xxhashjs) and other WASM hash packages
workload: Hash throughput at 32-byte and 1 MB inputs (MD5, SHA1, SHA256, SHA3-512, XXHash64) plus PBKDF2-SHA512 and Argon2id ops/s, in Chrome via the hash-wasm-benchmark app
claimed_speedup: 1 MB throughput: MD5 850.31 MB/s vs spark-md5 171.73 and crypto-js 46.71 MB/s; SHA256 426.16 vs noble-hashes 110.02, crypto-js 65.17 MB/s; SHA3-512 234.40 vs noble-hashes 14.19 MB/s; XXHash64 15 989 MB/s vs xxhashjs 42.26 MB/s; PBKDF2-SHA512 588 ops vs crypto-js 29 ops; Argon2id 438 ops vs argon2-browser 213 ops
compiler_and_flags: clang --target=wasm32 -flto -O3 -nostdlib -fno-builtin -ffreestanding (scripts/Makefile-clang, built in an Alpine 3.20.3 Docker image, compiler version not pinned); no WASM SIMD flags enabled (commented out in the Makefile)
tradeoffs: Each algorithm ships as a separate base64-embedded WASM binary, so there is a WASM instantiation cost on first use. Async init for the streaming createXXXX() API. Browsers and Node.js only.
caveats: The README table lists numbers for the README-stated library versions (hash-wasm 4.10.0) while the latest commit is 4.12.0. Numbers are first-party, produced by the author's own benchmark app (separate repo Daninet/hash-wasm-benchmark, source in src/ opened; the live app lives on github.io which was not reachable). Compiler version is not pinned. Node's native crypto module (OpenSSL) is not in the comparison, so this does not show it beats native hashing. XXHash64 1 MB figure (15 989 MB/s) is about equal to xxhash-wasm 1.0.2 (15 929 MB/s).
found_via: GitHub: README of Daninet/hash-wasm surfaced through the webassembly hash-library angle; benchmark section opened via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: xxhash-wasm
baseline: xxhashjs (pure JavaScript, 64-bit emulated via cuint) in Node/V8; also Node built-in crypto md5 and sha1
workload: Benchmark.js ops/sec hashing random strings from 1 byte to 100,000,000 bytes (32-bit and 64-bit xxHash)
claimed_speedup: xxhash-wasm 32-bit up to 90 times faster and 64-bit up to 350 times faster than xxhashjs; at 1 byte 4,438,501 ops/sec (64-bit) vs xxhashjs 11,896 ops/sec (64-bit); vs Node crypto md5 342,924 ops/sec at 1 byte; at 100,000,000 bytes 34.56 ops/sec vs xxhashjs 0.13 ops/sec (64-bit)
compiler_and_flags: wasm-opt --enable-bulk-memory -O4 src/xxhash.wat -o src/xxhash.wasm (package.json build-wasm script); benchmarks in the repo bench/ folder via Benchmark.js
hardware: x64 MacBook Pro (exact CPU model not stated), Node 17.3 for the Node-crypto table; hardware and Node version of the xxhashjs table not stated
tradeoffs: Needs async WebAssembly instance creation (about 2 ms in Node, about 1 ms in the browser) before first use. 64-bit API uses BigInt, which adds overhead for small inputs. Non-cryptographic hash only.
caveats: The headline ratio is against xxhashjs, a slow pure-JS port that emulates 64-bit math with cuint, not against a tuned JS hash. The Node crypto comparison is md5 and sha1, not another non-cryptographic hash. No official native xxHash C baseline in the table. Hardware only partly stated.
found_via: GitHub: topic webassembly hash libraries; README Comparison to xxhashjs section

name: json-as
baseline: JavaScript's built-in JSON.parse / JSON.stringify in V8 (and fast-json and assemblyscript-json in a library comparison)
workload: Serialize and deserialize nine classic payloads (Twitter 467 KB, Canada 2.1 MB, CITM 500 KB, Poet 3.3 MB, GitHub 53 KB, GSOC 3.1 MB, Lottie 289 KB, otfcc 66.4 MB, FGO 48.8 MB) in NAIVE, SWAR and SIMD scan modes against native JSON in a fresh V8
claimed_speedup: README states multi-GB/s (de)serialization and compares against V8's native JSON in charts; the per-payload numbers exist only in SVG charts on the docs branch (not readable as text), and string serialization with JSON_CACHE is stated as possibly in excess of 22 GB/s
compiler_and_flags: asc (AssemblyScript compiler) with JSON_MODE NAIVE/SWAR/SIMD; wasm-opt -O4 only in the asc-versus-warpo comparison; exact asc flags are in the repo bench scripts (not read)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 7800X3D (8 cores, 96 MB 3D V-Cache), 32 GB RAM, Zorin OS 18.1 (Linux 6.17); V8 with turboshaft
tradeoffs: Requires a compile-time transform and @json class decorators; schema-typed parsing, not arbitrary JSON (a dynamic JSON.Obj path exists). SIMD mode needs the WASM SIMD feature; the lazy-field path defers parsing work.
caveats: The current README shows only chart images, so no text-verifiable speedup number was extractable; an older README snapshot seen only in a search snippet reported roughly 6x to 11.5x serialization ops/s for simple values and up to about 44x for a typed object, which could not be re-checked here. Public bench/ folder, stated CPU and V8 runner suggest the tier could rise to A if the verifier can read the charts or rerun npm run bench:as and bench:js. Results include destination allocation. Author's own benchmarks only.
found_via: WebSearch: AssemblyScript library benchmark faster than JavaScript JSON.parse json-as; GitHub topic assemblyscript (sorted by stars)

name: TensorFlow.js WebAssembly backend (tfjs-backend-wasm)
baseline: TensorFlow.js plain JavaScript CPU backend in V8 (Chrome); also compared with the WebGL backend
workload: MobileNet V2 and Face Detector model inference time in ms (average of 200 runs) on iPhone X, Pixel 4, desktop Windows and Linux machines, Chrome 79
claimed_speedup: MobileNet V2: WASM backend about 3X-11.5X faster than the plain JS backend (ThinkPad X1 Gen6 Linux 122.7 ms WASM vs 1489.4 ms plain JS; WASM + SIMD 34.6 ms; WASM + SIMD + threads 12.4 ms); Face Detector: about 8.2X-19.8X faster (Desktop Linux 12.6 ms vs 249.5 ms plain JS)
compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the README beyond: built with the Bazel Emscripten toolchain; wraps the XNNPACK library; separate plain, simd, and threaded-simd binaries
hardware: iPhone X, Pixel 4, desktop Windows, ThinkPad X1 Gen6 Linux, desktop Linux; CPU models not stated; Chrome 79.0
tradeoffs: Separate WASM binaries for SIMD and threading need custom hosting and cross-origin isolation for threads. Slower than the WebGL backend on MobileNet V2 (about 5.3X-7.7X slower per README). Float32 CPU-style kernels.
caveats: 2020-era numbers on Chrome 79; the benchmark page (tfjs-benchmarks.web.app) is first-party and not reproducible from the README alone. Latest commit to the backend path dated April 2024. The plain-JS baseline is the same project's own unoptimized CPU backend.
found_via: WebSearch: tfjs-backend-wasm faster than plain JavaScript CPU backend benchmark SIMD speedup

name: Cheerp
workload: Vendor release-note comparison of compiled benchmark execution speed on one benchmark machine, averaged over three runs (snippet only; the post could not be opened)
claimed_speedup: Cheerp 2.6rc1 release notes (search snippet): Cheerp output runs roughly 5% faster than Emscripten; Cheerp 3.0 post (snippet): about 7% smaller output and execution speed comparable to Emscripten
tradeoffs: Compiles C++ to WebAssembly and JavaScript; the vendor 3.0 post says multithreading and WebAssembly atomics were not yet supported at 3.0. Different JS/DOM interop model than Emscripten (can call DOM directly).
caveats: Snippet only: leaningtech.com blog pages were EGRESS_BLOCKED, so the speed claim comes from WebSearch snippets of vendor posts. The newest vendor wording is parity with Emscripten, not faster; the only independent comparison found (Palant, 2016, asm.js era) had Emscripten slightly ahead. Neither the cheerp-compiler nor the cheerp-meta README contains a benchmark. Treat as weak: faster-in-size and about equal in speed.
found_via: WebSearch: Cheerp C++ WebAssembly compiler faster than Emscripten benchmark

name: markdown-wasm
baseline: markdown-it, marked, commonmark.js and showdown (pure JavaScript Markdown renderers) in NodeJS/V8
workload: Parse markdown and render HTML for a set of sample markdown files, averaged across files, single CPU thread, NodeJS v14.11.0
claimed_speedup: Average ops/second: markdown-wasm 195,065 vs markdown-it 84,774, marked 76,942, commonmark 66,185, showdown 8,502 (about 2.3x over markdown-it, derived from page data); average throughput 49 MB/s vs markdown-it 17 MB/s
compiler_and_flags: Built with the repo's wasmc tool (Emscripten based, wasmc.js sets only -DMD4C_USE_UTF8 and export flags in the release config); optimisation level not stated in the README
hardware: 2.9 GHz MacBook running macOS 10.15 (exact CPU model not stated), NodeJS v14.11.0
tradeoffs: Needs WASM instantiation; the WASM module is a wrapper over md4c (CommonMark parser written in C) so the speedup mainly reflects native md4c versus JS parsers. HTML-rendering API only, with a fixed option set.
caveats: Numbers were read from the README's SVG charts in test/benchmark/results (text inside the SVG, opened via raw.githubusercontent.com). Run on Node 14.11.0 in 2020; hardware only partly stated and compiler flags absent. The benchmark suite is public (npm run bench). Last commit July 2021, so comparisons predate current V8 and markdown-it releases.
found_via: GitHub: topic webassembly filtered to C (stars); README Benchmarks section; SVG charts under test/benchmark/results

name: md4w
baseline: markdown-it 14.0.0 (JavaScript) run under Deno; also markdown-wasm 1.2.1
workload: Render the CommonMark spec markdown file to HTML with Deno.bench (test/benchmark.js)
claimed_speedup: README: about 2.5x faster than markdown-it; the raw results exist only in test/benchmark-screenshot.png
compiler_and_flags: zig build: ReleaseFast for md4w-fast.wasm and ReleaseSmall for md4w-small.wasm, target wasm32-freestanding (build.zig); benchmark run with zig build && deno bench -A test/benchmark.js
tradeoffs: md4w-fast.wasm is 270KB gzipped (28KB for the slower md4w-small.wasm). Needs an async init(). Based on md4c, so CommonMark 0.31 compliant with partial GFM.
caveats: Speedup figure is only a headline in the README and a screenshot (not machine readable); hardware and Deno version not stated. The benchmark code is public and small (three Deno.bench cases), so a verifier can rerun it. markdown-wasm, also md4c-based, is in the same benchmark.
found_via: GitHub: topic webassembly filtered to Zig (stars); README Fast bullet and Benchmark section; test/benchmark.js read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: camaro
baseline: Pure-JavaScript XML parsers in Node.js/V8: txml, fast-xml-parser, xml-js, xml2js
workload: Transform a 60 KB Expedia hotel-list XML response to JSON with an XPath-like template (only the template's fields are extracted), mitata-style iterations
claimed_speedup: camaro v6 98.94 µs/iter vs txml 491.71 µs, xml-js 2.49 ms, fast-xml-parser 2.63 ms, xml2js 3.58 ms (5.27x, 25.78x, 24.21x and 37.02x faster per the README summary)
hardware: AMD 4650G, 6 cores / 12 threads, 32 GB memory (stated in the benchmark/ folder README per the folder page)
tradeoffs: Template-driven extraction rather than a general parse: output only contains requested fields. Small XML strings are probably slower than pure JavaScript parsers (README warning). Worker-thread pool for multi-core.
caveats: README itself says this is 'an unfair game for camaro' because it only transforms the fields in the template while the JS parsers build the whole tree. Benchmark code (benchmark/transform.js and fixtures) is public, but the README run's Node version is not stated and the raw benchmark README file could not be fetched via raw.githubusercontent.com (hardware line came from the GitHub folder page). Single fixture size.
found_via: GitHub: topic webassembly filtered to C++ (stars, page 2); README Benchmark section; build.sh read via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: as-proto
baseline: protobuf.js (reflect and static) and google-protobuf in Node.js/V8; also JSON string/buffer
workload: ts-proto's encode/decode benchmark on a small message, with an as-proto case added
claimed_speedup: Encoding: as-proto 1,295,297 ops/sec vs protobuf.js (static) 589,866 and (reflect) 589,073 (about 2.2x); combined encode+decode: 548,291 vs 439,242 and 421,963 ops/sec (about 1.3x); decoding is slower: 889,283 vs protobuf.js 1,375,425 and 1,308,310 ops/sec
hardware: Intel Core i7 2.2 GHz (MacBook Pro 2015); Node.js version not stated
tradeoffs: Generates AssemblyScript message classes from .proto files; no gRPC definitions. Decoding is slower than protobuf.js on the author's run. AssemblyScript's small GC is the usual limit on allocation-heavy paths.
caveats: Mixed result: wins encoding and the combined case, loses decoding by about 1.5x. Hardware is a 2015 laptop and AssemblyScript compiler flags are not stated; the benchmark comes from the ts-proto repo and is first-party for as-proto.
found_via: GitHub: topic assemblyscript (stars, page 3 and awesome-assemblyscript Serialization list); README Performance section

name: as-string-sink
baseline: JavaScript string concatenation (String += in V8, which uses ropes) and naive String += in AssemblyScript
workload: Append many short strings (100, 50,000 and 200,000) and measure total ms
claimed_speedup: 200,000 strings: JS String += 11.93 ms, AS String += 7622.72 ms, StringSink AS 2.88 ms (about 4.1x over JS, derived from page data); 50,000 strings: JS 3.34 ms vs StringSink 0.73 ms; README says up to 6 times faster than JS concat and up to 4000x faster than naive AS concatenation
tradeoffs: Buffer-based string builder with its own write/toString API; only helps accumulation patterns.
caveats: Tiny first-party microbenchmark: no hardware, runtime version or flags stated, the benchmark source was not opened, and at 100 strings the JS and AS plain concatenations (0.013 and 0.014 ms) are already near StringSink. The headline 4000x is against AssemblyScript's own naive concatenation, not JS.
found_via: GitHub: topic assemblyscript (stars, page 3); README Benchmark Results section

name: Zig wasm32-wasi build in msf/wasmplay
baseline: C++ compiled to WebAssembly with Emscripten (em++ -O2), run on the same WASM runtime; also Go (GOOS=wasip1) wasm
workload: 64x64 integer matrix multiplication with FNV-1a hash, 10,000 chained iterations, ops/sec, pinned to one core with taskset
claimed_speedup: Zig to WasmEdge 15,305 ops/sec vs C++ to WasmEdge 11,855 ops/sec (about 1.29x, derived from page data); Go to WasmEdge 3,230 ops/sec; Zig WASM described as nearly matching C++ optimized native (49,279 ops/sec native with -march=native)
compiler_and_flags: zig build-exe -O ReleaseFast -target wasm32-wasi; C++ side: em++ -std=c++20 -O2 (Makefile build-cpp-wasm); Go: GOOS=wasip1 GOARCH=wasm go build
hardware: AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX 370 (12 cores, 24 threads, up to 5.16 GHz), Ubuntu 24.04 (Linux 6.14.0-29-generic), single core pinned (CPU 0)
tradeoffs: Runs as WASI modules under WasmEdge, Wasmer or Wasmtime, not in a browser or V8; results depend on the runtime JIT (WasmEdge beat Wasmtime and Wasmer Cranelift for C++).
caveats: Unequal optimisation levels: the Zig WASM is ReleaseFast while the Emscripten C++ WASM is -O2 (the optimised -O3 -march=native C++ is only built for native). Single toy microbenchmark, one run per row, no variance. Not run in V8, so it does not show the TypeScript/JS baseline. The speedup between Zig and C++ is derived from the README bullet list.
found_via: WebSearch: Zig compiled to WebAssembly faster than JavaScript npm library benchmark (result for msf/wasmplay)

name: Almide
language: Almide (statically typed language compiling to Rust and WebAssembly)
baseline: Ordinary hand-written Rust (Box-linked recursive enum, no arena, rustc 1.96.1 opt-level=3, LTO, 1 codegen unit)
workload: Benchmarks-Game-style programs (binarytrees, treealloc, n-body, spectral-norm, fasta, FFT) on native output; wasm output measured as a ratio to native
claimed_speedup: binarytrees d17 134 ms vs ordinary Rust 382 ms (0.35x time), d19 581 vs 1826 ms (0.32x); treealloc d20 112 vs 375 ms, d21 221 vs 748 ms (0.30x); n-body and spectral-norm at 1.00x; fasta 1.16x and FFT 1.18x slower than Rust; wasm/native runtime ratios 1.04x to 1.96x for most benchmarks
compiler_and_flags: almide --release (emits Rust) vs handwritten Rust, both rustc opt-level=3 + LTO + 1 CGU; median of 9 interleaved runs after warmup; byte-identical stdout verified
hardware: Apple M4 Pro (arm64), almide 0.62.0, 2026-09-08; also an ubuntu-latest CI runner
tradeoffs: Young language optimised for LLM code generation; wins on allocation-heavy rows come from a compiler-proven region (bump-arena) window the ordinary Rust program does not have. Loses on fasta and FFT.
caveats: Baseline is not TypeScript/JS or C++/Emscripten: it is Rust, and the document states the ratio is allocator-dependent (binarytrees reads 0.61x on the ubuntu-latest CI runner because glibc frees a Box more cheaply than macOS). Only two workloads (binarytrees, treealloc) beat Rust, by one mechanism, and the M4 Pro columns were measured on 0.62.0 and not re-measured. Self-reported by the project; the benchmark scripts and raw JSON live in research/benchmark/perf. No JS/V8 comparison for the wasm output.
found_via: GitHub: topic webassembly filtered to Rust (updated); README performance section and docs/project/BENCHMARKS.md

name: AutoZig
baseline: JavaScript image filter in the browser; also Rust compiled to WASM ('Rust Native' row)
workload: Image filter (invert/grayscale style) over a 2.1 MB RGBA image, Zig @Vector SIMD128 compiled into a single .wasm with Rust
claimed_speedup: AutoZig (Zig SIMD) 0.80 ms (2631.84 MB/s) vs Rust 2.50 ms (842.19 MB/s, 3.13x slower) vs JavaScript 3.80 ms (554.07 MB/s, 4.75x slower); README headline 3-5x faster than pure JavaScript
compiler_and_flags: Zig -O ReleaseFast (README) / ReleaseSmall (example doc) + wasm-opt, target wasm32-freestanding, SIMD128; exact JS and Rust build flags not stated
tradeoffs: Combines Rust (memory and wasm-bindgen glue) with Zig compute kernels in one .wasm; needs the Zig toolchain at build time.
caveats: Single run on one image; browser, hardware, iteration count and JS implementation not stated. The Rust row appears to be scalar WASM without SIMD, so the 3x over 'Rust native' mostly measures SIMD128 versus scalar. Trivially vectorizable byte filter. Crate 0.1.2 with 80 downloads at lookup time. First-party only.
found_via: WebSearch: Zig compiled to WebAssembly faster than JavaScript (autozig README); crates.io API lookup for the repository URL

name: MoonBit
baseline: Go compiled to WebAssembly and Rust compiled to WebAssembly (vendor comparison); not TypeScript/JS in V8
workload: Vendor blog and news coverage (snippets only): fib(46) run ten million times, compile time for 626 packages, and WASM output size for hello-world programs
claimed_speedup: Snippet only: fib(46) x10M: MoonBit 177.9 ms, Rust 160.8 ms, Go 6357.8 ms (faster than Go wasm, not faster than Rust); compiles 626 packages in 1.06 s, about 9x faster than Rust; HTTP hello-world wasm 27KB vs 100KB Rust
tradeoffs: Wasm-first language with its own toolchain (moon build system); the core library is Apache-2.0 and the repo page does not state whether the compiler source is open. Young ecosystem.
caveats: Snippet only: moonbitlang.com and thenewstack.io pages were not reachable, so numbers come from WebSearch result summaries of vendor posts and secondary coverage and could not be checked. The repo's bench/ folder holds a benchmarking helper library, not published results. Runtime is slower than Rust in the one test quoted and no JavaScript/V8 comparison was found.
